_comment: Room Program canon — period-grounded room/building sizing for Structure Generation v2. MEDIEVAL frame: sizes derive from the BAY (the structural module between cross-frames) + house typology, NOT from modern residential area tables. Units = CUBES (1 cube = 1 m). Every value carries a `sources` entry (the grounding rule). 'bays' on a room = how many structural bays it occupies. See docs/structure-generation/StructureBrief.md + docs/structure-generation/StructureGenerationV2.md. Modern 1500/2100 sq ft figures DO NOT apply here.
_units: cubes (metres). bay_length/width in cubes; 'bays' = structural-bay count.
_wealth_tier_note: wealth_tier (humble|middling|high) drives the tier-filtered furnishing recipes (resources/furnishing_recipes.json). REASONED status mapping, not a cited fact: peasant dwellings (croft/longhouse) = humble; the yeoman hall house + town trades (tavern/shops) = middling; the manor = high. Status, not function, is the real medieval driver of household goods.

croft.description: Single-room peasant cottage — one 'house' room with a central hearth.
croft.source: Wharram Percy / vernacular cruck cottage; cruck dwelling width <=6 m

sources.width_max: crucks for houses/barns 'no more than 6 m (20 ft) wide' (buildingconservation.com timber-framed buildings)
sources.bay_length: DERIVED ~4 m: 4-bay longhouse 15-18 m / 4 (Wikipedia Longhouse, Germanic 50-60 ft); canonical module per Brunskill, Timber Building in England (1985) — TBD
sources.bays: 1-2 bay peasant cottage (Wharram Percy excavation, Beresford & Hurst)
sources.entrance: long-wall entry by FAMILY ANALOGY to the cross-passage forms (Dartmoor longhouse / hall house opposed long-wall doorways); croft-specific position along the wall NEEDS-RESEARCH (Brunskill 1971 plates; Beresford & Hurst Wharram Percy building plans) — wall middle is the disclosed default (grounding-auditor 2026-07-06)
sources.windows.count: humble tier 0-2, door + windows sharing the sun-facing long wall: NOSAS survey of a cruck cottage near Beauly — 'a doorway and two windows in the south wall', the north window a later insertion (⚠ verify: single Scottish Highland site); 'Single room dwellings often did not even have window openings' (Herefordshire Through Time). per_bay 0.5 on the front wall ≈ 1 per 2-bay croft, inside the attested 0-2 band (grounding-auditor 2026-07-06)
sources.windows.size: STYLIZED — NO metric source for a humble window opening (the 12-18 in figure is 11th-c castle windows, wrong class); 1x1 cube = the smallest carvable opening on the cube portal grid, KNOWN OVERSIZED vs the qualitative 'small shuttered opening' record; pending Brunskill (1971) / Weald & Downland build records / HE HEAG102. Openings are SHUTTERED AIR, never Glass: glazing unaffordable for ordinary households before Elizabeth I (1558+) (buildingconservation.com early-casement article)

tower_house.description: Tower house / tower keep — a compact thick-walled stone tower: a store at ground, the hall above it, private chambers stacked over that, reached by a generated stair. The lord's fortified residence, and the keep form this engine can actually structure. CityForgePlan M8.
tower_house.source: Tower house — GROUNDED MINIMUM 6.1 x 4.9 x 12.2 m (20 x 16 x 40 ft), the dimensional standard set by the Henry VI statute of 1429 for the Irish '£10 castles'. Stacked single rooms over a vaulted store is the defining plan. Full sheet: docs/structure-generation/archetypes/tower_house.md

sources.width_min: the 1429 statute's 4.9 m short side is the attested MINIMUM; 5 cubes is that minimum, 8 the upper end of the compact tower form
sources.bays: 2 bays x 4 m = 8 m long, against the statute's 6.1 m minimum long side — inside the real range for a compact tower
sources.stories: 3: the statute's 12.2 m height over a vaulted store implies 3-4 stacked floors. Rooms STACK (one per floor) — that is the tower plan, not a simplification
sources.rooms: one room per floor. Ground = the store/vault ('service' recipe); the hall and the private chambers above are generated stories ('chamber' -> the bedchamber recipe). Both recipes are already conformant — no new assets
sources._not_modelled: DISCLOSED deviations from the sheet, none faked: (1) the FIRST-FLOOR ENTRANCE with a removable stair, and a ground vault with no external door, are the tower's defining defensive trick — the engine doors every building at ground level, so this tower is entered at the bottom; (2) no mural/spiral stair in the wall thickness (the generated stair is a normal one); (3) no crenellated parapet on the roof (buildings get roofs, not battlements — the town WALL has crenellations); (4) no vaulting.
sources._why_not_a_great_tower: The Dover/Rochester-scale KEEP (docs/structure-generation/archetypes/keep.md, 21-30 m square) is NOT shipped, and not because of a width cap — widthMax is per-typology data. A great tower of that span needs an internal CROSS-WALL (which is exactly why Rochester and Dover have one: floors cannot span the full width). This engine's room model divides a plan along the LONG axis only, so every room would be full-width and a 14 m clear span would be implied. That is a mechanism gap, logged in docs/StructurePipelineGaps.md, not something to fake with a wide empty box.

town_hall.description: Moot hall / town house — the seat of town government: a public hall at ground with a secure muniment (records + town arms) beside it, and the council chamber above reached by a generated stair. CityForgePlan M5.
town_hall.source: Market-house form (civic hall over a public ground floor) — Thaxted Guildhall (Essex, c.1450) and Ledbury Market House (Herefordshire, 1617) are the surviving type. Full sheet: docs/structure-generation/archetypes/town_hall.md

sources.rooms: the archetype's required spaces are a public/market floor + the civic hall + a secure muniment/armoury (town_hall.md §5). Ground public_hall and the generated upper council chamber both use the CIVIC recipe (council board + benches + chair of office + muniment chest + candle stand); muniment/armoury use 'service' (chests, barrels). All pieces are already-conformant assets — no new assets.
sources._civic_has_no_hearth: USER-SETTLED 2026-08-28: the town hall skips the fireplace — do not re-litigate. Background: the sheet lists a hearth in the civic hall, but a ground-floor stack rises through the middle of the council chamber above and the realizer's flue gate REFUSES it ('no silent lean'). Rather than fake a chimney or drop the upper hall, the civic recipe ships hearthless. (The general hearth-siting improvement is still logged in docs/StructurePipelineGaps.md for OTHER typologies; it is no longer needed for this one.)
sources.width_max: 7 m = the timber-frame span this engine builds (shared with hall_house/tavern); Thaxted Guildhall is ~6 m wide, so the type genuinely fits the span — no aisled frame needed for a MOOT hall (a grand arcaded town hall would)
sources.bays: 4 bays ~= 16 m long: Thaxted Guildhall's three-storey range and Ledbury's 17-bay market house bracket it; REASONED within that range, not measured
sources.stories: 2: public floor + civic hall above, the defining market-house arrangement (CITED, town_hall.md)
sources._not_modelled: DISCLOSED omissions vs the archetype sheet: the OPEN ARCADE ground floor (the realizer has no open-story/column mechanism — the engine builds an enclosed public hall instead), the bell turret, and the lock-up cell. Each is a mechanism gap, not a data gap; none is faked.

tenement.description: Urban rental row unit ('rents') — two storeys, one room per floor: an all-purpose ground room (hearth, table, chest) with a single chamber above, gable to the street; rows form by contiguous burgage packing. CityForgePlan M4 — the medieval 'apartment'.
tenement.source: Our Lady's Row, Goodramgate, York (1316) — England's earliest surviving purpose-built rental row: two storeys, ONE ROOM PER FLOOR per unit. Full sheet: docs/structure-generation/archetypes/tenement.md

sources.rooms: one room up, one room down per dwelling — the documented Our Lady's Row unit plan (Wikipedia, Our Lady's Row; RCHME York vol. 5). Ground purpose REUSES the croft 'living' recipe; upper REUSES the inn 'bedchamber' recipe — both conformant, no new assets (REFUSE-ON-ANY-GAP satisfied by construction)
sources.stories: two storeys, jettied — CITED for Our Lady's Row (jetty itself NOT modelled; disclosed in the sheet, never faked)
sources.width_min: unit frontage ~4.5-5.5 m (≈15-18 ft, commonly quoted for Our Lady's Row — NEEDS-VERIFY vs RCHME before citing as measured); engine 4-5 stays inside that envelope
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION, disclosed: the documented ~4.5 m unit depth cannot host the forge's generated stair (the traversal gate would refuse); 2 bays x 4 m gives the stair an honest run. Medieval ladder-stairs are not modelled
sources.entrance: DESIGN DECISION, disclosed: gable-to-street (narrow-frontage burgage economics + core packing); Our Lady's Row itself runs eaves-on — the allocator's contiguous packing recreates the ROW read either way

longhouse.description: Peasant longhouse — dwelling end (inner room + hall) + cross passage + byre, under one roof.
longhouse.source: Dartmoor / Wharram Percy longhouse (Wikipedia Longhouse; English Heritage Wharram Percy)

sources.bays: Dartmoor longhouse = 'two crucked bays, a cross passage, and two crucked bays' (Wikipedia Longhouse)
sources.length: Germanic longhouse '50 to 60 feet long' = 15-18 m (Wikipedia Longhouse)
sources.rooms: inner room (sleeping/dairy) + living room w/ central hearth + cross passage + byre (English Heritage, Wharram Percy)
sources.entrance: cross passage between the dwelling end and the byre = the 4-bay midpoint ('two crucked bays, a cross passage, and two crucked bays' — Wikipedia Dartmoor longhouse; EH Wharram Percy: inner room + hall + cross passage + byre). OPPOSED pair: 'opposed doorways on the front and back walls' (Wikipedia Dartmoor longhouse); 'two opposing doors...connected by a passage' (Wikipedia Byre-dwelling). Topology fix, bay-aligned, zero rounding (grounding-auditor 2026-07-06)
sources.windows.count: same humble-tier 0-2 / front-wall band as croft (NOSAS Beauly survey; Herefordshire Through Time)
sources.windows.size: STYLIZED — same caveat as croft (no metric source; 1x1 cube = smallest carvable, oversized; shuttered air, no Glass pre-1558)
sources.windows.byre: byre gets NO windows — REASONED, not attested: the byre record mentions only a dung-shovel aperture + drain (Legendary Dartmoor; Wikipedia Byre-dwelling); absence-of-mention is not proof (grounding-auditor 2026-07-06)

hall_house.description: Yeoman/gentry hall house — open hall (middle two bays) flanked by service (lower) and solar (upper) ends.

sources.bays: 'four-bay cruck-framed structure, with the open hall taking up the two bays in the middle' (Wikipedia Hall house)
sources.rooms: open hall (middle 2 bays) + service end + solar (Wikipedia Hall house)
sources.example: c.1530 hall house 14.2 m x 6.7 m (Wikipedia Hall house, Rufford Old Hall, built for Sir Robert Hesketh)
sources.entrance: screens passage at the LOW end, between service and hall: 'two external doors on each side of the hall formed a cross passage' (Wikipedia Hall house / Great hall) — 1 bay in from the gable, bay-aligned (grounding-auditor 2026-07-06)
sources.windows.count: STYLIZED count by family analogy (no dimensioned hall-house window survey found this pass; middling-tier sizes NEEDS-RESEARCH — Rufford Old Hall conservation report / Brunskill). Shutters only: glazing gated post-1558 for ordinary households (buildingconservation.com); the Stokesay part-glazed pattern is reserved for manor_hall status
sources.windows.size: STYLIZED — same 1x1-cube smallest-carvable caveat as croft

tavern._grounding_note: The room PROGRAM (a public common room + kitchen + service/storage end) is grounded in the medieval-inn record. The BAY FRAME (4 bays, 2+1+1 split) is an explicit DESIGN DECISION by analogy to the grounded hall_house ground floor, NOT a measured inn — no inn-specific bay count was sourced (would need Pantin, 'Medieval Inns', Studies in Building History 1961). Upstairs lodging (guest chambers) is added by multi-story generation.
tavern.description: Town inn / tavern — ground floor: public taproom (the common room, 2 bays) + kitchen + service/storage end, on the timber-frame bay system. Upper floor: guest chambers (lodging), reached by a generated stair.
tavern.source: Medieval inn room program (Medievalists.net) + timber-frame hall-house frame (Wikipedia Hall house / Great hall) as the modelling analogy

sources.rooms: medieval inn = main hall / common room + kitchen + chambers + innkeeper's quarters + stables + common area ('Ye Ol' Bed & Breakfast', Medievalists.net 2015). The taproom = the public common room; the service/storage end is general medieval building practice (not attributed to that article).
sources.width_max: DOCUMENTED framed hall-house footprint c.1530 = 14.2 m x 6.7 m wide -> 7 m (Wikipedia Hall house, Rufford Old Hall: '46.5 feet (14.2 m) long and 22 feet (6.7 m) wide', built for Sir Robert Hesketh c.1530). NOT the unsourced '8 m framed hall' claim.
sources.width_min: cruck dwelling <=6 m (buildingconservation.com, timber-framed buildings) — lower bound of the framed range
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not an inn measurement): modelled on the grounded hall_house 4-bay frame, inn ground floor ~= a hall. Taproom = the 2 middle bays (cf. hall_house open hall = middle 2 bays, Wikipedia Hall house); kitchen + store one bay each. No inn-specific bay count was sourced.
sources.bay_length: ~4 m timber-frame bay module shared with croft/longhouse/hall_house (DERIVED; same Brunskill 1985 TBD caveat as those entries)
sources.stories: 2 storeys: ground-floor public rooms + upper-floor guest chambers — the standard town-inn lodging form. Attested: The New Inn, Gloucester is a three-storey galleried inn with chambers on the upper floors (Wikipedia). 2 is the conservative town-tavern default; multi-story gen supports more. (Medievalists.net grounds the inn room programme — hall/chambers/kitchen — but not the vertical placement.)
sources.example_for_TYPE_only: The New Inn, Gloucester (timber-framed galleried courtyard inn, c.1430-50, ~40 chambers; Wikipedia) attests medieval inns as multi-storey galleried buildings with many guest chambers — evidence for the TYPE + the upstairs-lodging direction, NOT for this 4-bay scale (it is a large 7-bay courtyard inn).
sources.windows.count: STYLIZED by analogy to the hall-house family — no inn-specific window survey (would need Pantin, Medieval Inns, 1961); per_bay 1.0 on the street front (urban shopfront tier more fenestrated than the rural humble tier is a REASONED, unattested step). Shutters only per the 1558 glazing gate (buildingconservation.com); upper-floor chamber windows consistent with domestic upper-floor 'weavers' windows' precedent (Wikipedia Weavers' windows)
sources.windows.size: STYLIZED — same 1x1-cube smallest-carvable caveat as croft; middling/shopfront opening dims NEEDS-RESEARCH (Pantin shop-front studies; Schofield & Vince, Medieval Towns)
sources.sign_item: THAT an inn hangs a sign over its entrance is attested — a 1393 statute of Richard II required ale-sellers to display a sign, and the painted board on an alestake/bracket is the standard form (Wikipedia, Pub names / Alestake). WHICH sign is art direction, NOT a measured value: 'The Prancing Pony' is simply the authored asset (resources/templates/items/sign_prancing_pony.voxel). What IS grounded is the MOUNT — see RealizedStructureValidator::checkSignClearance (>=8 ft board clearance, <=48 in projection, above the door head).

blacksmith._grounding_note: Program (forge floor on the forge->anvil->quench work triangle + a customer-facing storefront/yard) grounded in the smithing record (Beautiful Iron, Wikipedia Forge). FOOTPRINT scale anchored to an EXCAVATED smithy: the Jamestown (James Fort) metalworking structure was 16x20 ft = 4.9x6.1 m (Historic Jamestowne archaeology, 2006). That grounds the forge-WORKSPACE scale (~5x6 m, one ~4 m bay wide); the 2nd bay (the customer storefront) is a disclosed DESIGN DECISION by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay (croft/longhouse/hall_house) -- the same honest basis as the tavern bay frame. (An earlier draft mis-cited the Anderson shop, Colonial Williamsburg; that text was not on the cited page -- corrected to Jamestown.) See docs/structure-generation/archetypes/blacksmith.md.
blacksmith.description: Village smithy -- open-fronted single-story timber-frame workshop: forge floor (forge on the vented back wall, anvil within a step, quench/slack tub beside it) + a customer-facing storefront/yard. Fire-managed: non-combustible around the forge.
blacksmith.source: Blacksmith/forge program (beautifuliron.com forge planning; Wikipedia Forge) + Jamestown excavated smithy footprint scale (Historic Jamestowne) + the ~4 m timber-frame bay as the modelling analogy

sources.rooms: the forge->anvil->quench work triangle on a fire-safe forge floor (beautifuliron.com/forge_planning.htm; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forge) + a customer-facing storefront/yard (medieval smithy mixed-use). forge_floor T1 (smith-only), storefront T0 (customers).
sources.width_max: <=6 m: cruck dwelling/workshop width 'no more than 6 m' (buildingconservation.com); matches the Jamestown smithy ~4.9-6.1 m footprint
sources.width_min: 5 m: a working forge floor + clearance around the anvil work triangle (DESIGN, lower end of the framed range; ~ the Jamestown 4.9 m short side)
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not a surveyed 2-room smithy): bay 1 = forge floor at ~Jamestown workspace scale (~4x5.5 m); bay 2 = customer storefront ADDED by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay. The Jamestown smithy (16x20 ft) was a single forge cellar, not a 2-room shop -- the storefront is the disclosed design addition.
sources.bay_length: ~4 m timber-frame bay module shared with croft/longhouse/hall_house (DERIVED; Brunskill 1985 TBD caveat)
sources.proportion_max: 2.5 DESIGN: keeps the 2-bay plan from elongating past a usable storefront-to-forge depth (no surveyed ratio; cf. manor_hall's cited 1.5-3x for great halls)
sources.stories: 1 storey: the village smithy is a single open-fronted workshop (mixed-use dwelling above is a HIGH-status variant, not the default; archetype sheet sec.9). Fire risk favours keeping the forge floor on the ground, often detached.
sources.footprint_example_for_SCALE_only: Jamestown (James Fort) metalworking structure, 'rectangular, 16 feet by 20 feet' = 4.9x6.1 m, a forge shop c.1608 later converted to a bakery (Historic Jamestowne, map-of-discoveries/blacksmith-shopbakery) -- an EXCAVATED smithy, evidence for the workspace SCALE, not this 2-room plan.

general_store._grounding_note: Program (a street-facing SALESROOM at the front of the burgage plot + a STOREROOM behind) is grounded in the medieval urban-shop record: the front of a burgage plot facing the street was the business space (shop/workshop), with storage/living to the rear (RuralHistoria; burgageplots.info 'the burgage plot as a workplace'). FOOTPRINT scale anchored to documented burgage FRONTAGE: plot widths ran c. 5 m (one perch) to ~17 m, MODAL ~8 m / typical 2 perches ~10 m, lengths tens of metres (Tait, 'Burgage plot patterns and dimensions in four Scottish burghs', PSAS 138 (2009), journals.socantscot.org/.../view/9724). A general store = the NARROW end of that range (~5-6 m / 1-1.2 perch frontage), NOT the typical 8-10 m. The 2-bay depth (~8 m) is a disclosed DESIGN DECISION by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay (croft/longhouse/hall_house) and sits well within documented plot depths (tens of m) -- same honest basis as the tavern/blacksmith bay frame. (grounding-auditor 2026-06-28: corrected the PSAS citation from the Edinburgh-only paper /9686 to the four-burgh paper /9724, and the frontage floor from a 5.5 m misread of '5.5 yards' to ~5 m = one perch 5.03 m.)
general_store.description: Town general store / merchant's shop -- single-story timber building on a burgage frontage: a street-facing salesroom (sales counter + shelved goods + barrels) and a storeroom behind (stock: barrels, crates, coffers).
general_store.source: Medieval urban shop / burgage-plot record (RuralHistoria; burgageplots.info) + documented burgage frontage dimensions (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009) four-burgh paper, journals.socantscot.org/.../view/9724) + the ~4 m timber-frame bay as the modelling analogy

sources.rooms: front of the burgage plot (street frontage) = the business space -- shop/workshop/tavern; storage + living to the rear (ruralhistoria.com/2023/12/04/what-is-a-medieval-burgage-plot; burgageplots.info/the-burgage-plot-as-a-workplace). salesroom = the shopfront (customer-facing, T0); storeroom = rear stock (T1).
sources.width_min: 5 m: the NARROW end of documented burgage frontage = ONE PERCH (5.5 yards / 16.5 ft = 5.03 m), the documented minimum frontage unit (burgageplots.info; cf. Birmingham burgage plots 'about five metres wide', sarahhayes.org). The Tait PSAS 138 (2009) four-burgh modal frontage is 8 m (quarter-plot steps from 6 m), so 5 m sits just below Tait's smallest step, on the perch/Birmingham basis. A small urban shop sits at the narrow end; the TYPICAL frontage was ~2 perches / 8-10 m.
sources.width_max: 6 m (~1.2 perch): still the NARROW end of the c. 5-17 m documented frontage range, modal ~8 m (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009) /view/9724); also <= the cruck-workshop 6 m max (buildingconservation.com)
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not a surveyed 2-room shop): bay 1 = street salesroom, bay 2 = rear storeroom, by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay. The burgage record grounds the FRONT-business / REAR-storage split + the frontage width, not a specific bay count.
sources.bay_length: ~4 m timber-frame bay module shared with croft/longhouse/hall_house (DERIVED; Brunskill 1985 TBD caveat)
sources.proportion_max: 2.5 DESIGN: keeps the 2-bay plan from elongating past a usable shop depth; ~8 m deep sits within the documented 10 m+ burgage plot length (no surveyed shop ratio; cf. blacksmith 2.5)

bakery._grounding_note: Program (a BAKEHOUSE with the masonry oven + a kneading/work surface, and a customer SALESROOM/shopfront selling the bread) is grounded in the medieval baking record: the bakehouse was the dedicated oven-room workspace (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakehouse_(building)); commercial bakers baked and SOLD bread under the Assize of Bread, so a town bakery has a shopfront as well as the bakehouse (RuralHistoria burgage front-business pattern). FOOTPRINT on a burgage frontage like the general_store (documented 5-17 m, narrow-end shop ~6 m; Tait PSAS 138 (2009)). The OVEN is the grounded commercial dome (object_dimensions 'oven_bread': ~0.9 m interior, williamrubel.com), VENTED on the back wall + chimney (place_chimney), fire-managed like the forge. The 2-bay frame is a disclosed DESIGN DECISION (~4 m timber bay analogy) -- same honest basis as tavern/blacksmith/general_store.
bakery.description: Town bakery -- single-story timber building on a burgage frontage: a bakehouse (the vented masonry bread oven + a kneading counter + flour barrels) and a street salesroom selling the bread.
bakery.source: Medieval bakehouse + baker's-shop record (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakehouse_(building); Assize of Bread) + commercial dome-oven dimensions (williamrubel.com; object_dimensions 'oven_bread') + burgage frontage (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009)) + the ~4 m timber bay analogy

sources.rooms: the bakehouse = the dedicated oven workspace (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakehouse_(building)); a commercial baker sold bread from a shopfront (Assize of Bread regulated baker's sale; burgage front-business pattern, ruralhistoria.com). bakehouse T1 (the oven/work), salesroom T0 (customers).
sources.width_min: 5 m: a narrow urban shop at ~one perch (5.5 yd = 5.03 m, the documented minimum burgage unit, burgageplots.info; cf. Birmingham burgage plots 'about five metres wide', sarahhayes.org). The Tait PSAS 138 (2009) four-burgh modal frontage is 8 m (quarter-plot steps from 6 m); 5 m is the perch/Birmingham narrow end. The bakehouse must still seat the 1.6 m oven + clearance.
sources.width_max: 6 m (~1.2 perch): narrow end of the c. 5-17 m frontage range (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009)); <= the cruck-workshop 6 m max (buildingconservation.com)
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not a surveyed 2-room bakery): bay 1 = bakehouse (oven + kneading), bay 2 = street salesroom, by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay. The record grounds the bakehouse/oven + the baker selling bread, not a specific bay count.
sources.bay_length: ~4 m timber-frame bay module shared with croft/longhouse/hall_house (DERIVED; Brunskill 1985 TBD caveat)
sources.proportion_max: 2.5 DESIGN: keeps the 2-bay plan from over-elongating (cf. blacksmith/general_store 2.5; no surveyed bakery ratio)

apothecary._grounding_note: Program (a DISPENSARY/shopfront -- a dispensing counter with shelves of labeled jars/bottles BEHIND it -- plus a rear STOREROOM for stock) is grounded in the apothecary-shop record: 'drug jars lined shelves behind the counter where prescriptions were made up', the apothecary moving between customers and stock (manyheadedmonster.com 'The World in a Jar' -- EARLY MODERN England c.1550-1800; larsdatter.com = period image refs). PERIOD CAVEAT: the cited prose is early modern; the counter + shelved-jars dispensary form is plausibly medieval (albarello drug jars predate 1550) but not directly attested medieval -- evidence for the LAYOUT (cf. the tavern's New-Inn TYPE cite). FOOTPRINT on a burgage frontage like the general_store (Tait PSAS 138 (2009); narrow shop ~5-6 m). All fixtures reuse grounded assets (counter; back_bar shelving, which carries jars/bottles; coffer; candelabra for the dim apothecary light). The 2-bay frame is a disclosed DESIGN DECISION (~4 m timber bay analogy) -- same basis as the other shops.
apothecary.description: Town apothecary / herbalist -- single-story timber building on a burgage frontage: a dispensary (dispensing counter + shelves of jars/bottles behind + a coffer + a candelabra) and a rear storeroom of stock.
apothecary.source: Apothecary-shop layout record (manyheadedmonster.com 'The World in a Jar', EARLY MODERN c.1550-1800; larsdatter.com image refs) + burgage frontage (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009)) + the ~4 m timber bay analogy

sources.rooms: 'tin-glazed earthenware drug jars lined shelves BEHIND the counter where prescriptions were made up', the apothecary moving between customers and stock (manyheadedmonster.com/2021/04/13/the-world-in-a-jar). PERIOD CAVEAT: that source is EARLY MODERN England (c.1550-1800); the counter + shelved-jars dispensary form is plausibly medieval (albarello drug jars predate 1550) but this source does not directly attest the medieval period -- evidence for the LAYOUT, disclosed like the tavern's New-Inn TYPE cite. (grounding-auditor 2026-06-28: the quote is from manyheadedmonster, not larsdatter (an image aggregator); reordered + added the period disclosure.) dispensary = the counter + shelved jars (T0 customer-facing); storeroom = rear stock (T1).
sources.width_min: 5 m: a narrow urban shop at ~one perch (5.5 yd = 5.03 m, the documented minimum burgage unit, burgageplots.info); cf. Birmingham burgage plots 'about five metres wide' (sarahhayes.org). NOTE: the Tait PSAS 138 (2009) four-burgh modal frontage is 8 m (quarter-plot steps from 6 m); 5 m is the perch/Birmingham narrow end, below Tait's smallest step.
sources.width_max: 6 m (~1.2 perch): narrow end of the c. 5-17 m frontage range (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009)); <= cruck 6 m max (buildingconservation.com)
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not a surveyed 2-room apothecary): bay 1 = dispensary, bay 2 = rear storeroom, by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay. The record grounds the counter+shelved-jars dispensary, not a bay count.

butcher._grounding_note: Program (a street-facing SHAMBLES shopfront -- a stall-board/display counter, the chopping block, a rail of meat hooks -- with a back room for slaughter/storage) is grounded in the medieval butcher record: the Shambles were streets of butchers' shops 'many complete with a slaughterhouse at the back', with low display windowsills (stall boards) and meat-HOOKS on the shop fronts (historyofyork.org.uk/themes/medieval/the-shambles; asparadventures.com York Shambles). The chopping BLOCK is an attested trade tool (choppingblocks.com) but NOT quoted in those Shambles pages; interior meat RAILS are a Victorian-era form (buildingourpast.com), a disclosed post-medieval analogy. FOOTPRINT on a burgage frontage like the other shops (Tait PSAS 138 (2009); narrow ~5-6 m). 2-bay frame is a disclosed DESIGN DECISION (~4 m timber bay analogy).
butcher.description: Town butcher's shop (the shambles) -- single-story timber building on a burgage frontage: a shopfront (stall-board counter + chopping block + a rail of meat hooks) and a back room (slaughter/storage).
butcher.source: Medieval butcher / Shambles record (historyofyork.org.uk the-shambles; asparadventures.com; buildingourpast.com) + burgage frontage (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009)) + the ~4 m timber bay analogy

sources.rooms: Shambles = butchers' shops 'with a slaughterhouse at the back', 'shammels'/stall-board shop-fronts for display, and meat-HOOKS on the shop fronts (historyofyork.org.uk/themes/medieval/the-shambles; asparadventures.com/2018/04/20). The chopping BLOCK is an attested trade tool (choppingblocks.com) but is NOT quoted in those Shambles pages; interior meat RAILS are a Victorian-era form (buildingourpast.com), a disclosed post-medieval analogy. shopfront = the shambles (counter + block + meat rail, T0 customer-facing); backroom = slaughter/storage (T1). (grounding-auditor 2026-06-28: removed a misattributed wooden-block quote that was falsely pinned to historyofyork; flagged rails as Victorian.)
sources.width_min: 5 m: a narrow urban shop at ~one perch (5.5 yd = 5.03 m, the documented minimum burgage unit, burgageplots.info; cf. Birmingham burgage plots 'about five metres wide', sarahhayes.org). The Tait PSAS 138 (2009) four-burgh modal frontage is 8 m (quarter-plot steps from 6 m); 5 m is the perch/Birmingham narrow end.
sources.width_max: 6 m (~1.2 perch): narrow end of the c. 5-17 m frontage range, = Tait's smallest quarter-plot step 3/4 x 8 m (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009)); <= cruck 6 m max (buildingconservation.com)
sources.bays: DESIGN DECISION (analogy, not a surveyed 2-room butcher): bay 1 = shambles shopfront, bay 2 = back slaughter/storage, by analogy to the grounded ~4 m timber bay. The record grounds the shopfront-block-hooks + rear-slaughterhouse split, not a bay count.
